assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are a measurement instrument that changed what can be measured: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, relativistic redshifts resolved over millimetre scales, and a clear route to redefining the second. This is the kind of precision-measurement advance that opens new observations of nature (geodesy, fundamental-constant tests, dark-matter searches) and was demonstrated experimentally, not only proposed.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and first realised strontium lattice clocks; Ye's JILA group drove the systematic-uncertainty and stability records and the many-body clock work. Both are credited, which gives a clean two-person configuration. Credit for the underlying lattice-trapping ideas and for the Sr/Yb community is somewhat diffuse, but the decisive contributions are identifiable.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, others) have reproduced and surpassed each other for over a decade; the interpretation is stable and the recognition is timely. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, which is not necessary for the prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with frequency-comb recognition from 2005 and with ion-clock work from 2012 could be argued either way.
Whether the committee wants to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.
I am working from memory on precise uncertainty figures and have not verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision sensor for gravity, gravity gradients, rotation and the fine-structure constant, and underpins cold-atom gravimetry and tests of the equivalence principle. As an experimentalist I value the clear chain from an optics-like concept to instruments with demonstrated sensitivity and field applications.
assessment.attribution: Bordé's theory of light-pulse interferometry, Pritchard's early atom-optics and interferometer demonstrations, and Kasevich's (with Chu) gravimeter and gradiometer work are all central. Steven Chu already has the 1997 prize, which complicates and may lessen the need for his inclusion. The three-name set is plausible but the relative weight of Bordé versus Pritchard is debatable, and others (Chu, Rasel, Hänsch-era groups) could argue claims.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups and now commercial and field-deployed devices; large-scale space and long-baseline projects are still developing. Recognition is timely, with a mature core field.
uncertainties: Attribution is contested among several early groups and Chu's prior prize complicates credit.
Impact beyond a few specialist metrology uses is still developing, and the long-baseline fundamental-physics targets are not yet reached.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for trapped-ion quantum gates, together with the ensuing experimental realisation of ion-based logic gates and entanglement, laid a concrete hardware foundation for quantum computing and simulation. It is original, has lasting influence across platforms and links to precision measurement through ion control.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the clear theoretical originators; Blatt is a leading experimental demonstrator, but Wineland's group (already prized in 2012) and Monroe, Wineland and others were also decisive in early gates, so the experimental share is not uniquely Blatt's. The theory-plus-experiment trio is reasonable but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Well-confirmed with multiple independent platforms, now at commercial scale. The field was partly recognised in 2012, which may reduce the novelty of the recognition, but the theory proposal remains unrecognised.
uncertainties: Prior 2012 prize for ion control overlaps with this candidate.
Credit for the first experimental gate is shared with the NIST group.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light for quantum-enhanced measurement began as theory (Caves) and a laboratory demonstration (Kimble) and now operates in LIGO and Virgo, where it beats the standard quantum limit in a real instrument. This directly addresses my interest in how measurement precision limits knowledge, with a clear example of impact in a major detector.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed the interferometer squeeze idea, Kimble's group produced the first experimental squeezed states, and Schnabel led GEO600 and later broadband squeezing development. Mavalvala and others also contributed to the LIGO squeezing implementation; limiting to three means choosing between Schnabel and Mavalvala, which is contestable. Slusher's first squeezed-light observation also needs weighing.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed through gravitational-wave detector upgrades; the technology is routine. The conceptual origin dates to the 1980s, so this is a mature recognition, though the 2017 prize for gravitational waves may be thought to overlap in application.
uncertainties: Several credible contributors (Slusher, Walls, Mavalvala, Lam) remain outside any three-person set.
The 2017 gravitational-wave prize may be viewed as having covered part of the impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices implement tunable many-body Hamiltonians with single-site detection (quantum gas microscopes), providing a new way to observe strongly correlated matter. The Mott insulator transition and fermionic Hubbard-model studies are well-defined experimental milestones of lasting importance.
assessment.attribution: Greiner (with Hänsch and Bloch) observed the Mott insulator transition, Bloch pioneered lattice quantum simulation and microscopy, and Esslinger led the fermionic work. Zoller and Jaksch proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, so theory credit is a real issue and selecting three from four credited names excludes Zoller, which is an acknowledged cost.
assessment.maturity: Many groups have reproduced and extended these results; the field is mature, though quantitative advantage over classical simulation for open problems is still being established.
uncertainties: Zoller's theoretical role is left out of this set.
Whether the practical output of quantum simulation has yet reached Nobel-level discovery impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED supplies the architecture for most superconducting quantum processors and for quantum-limited readout, a measurement technique with large leverage across quantum information. It is original and has opened a large body of subsequent work.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf published the 2004 proposal and first experiments; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling in experiment. Girvin versus Blais is a close choice. The 2025 prize on macroscopic circuit quantum tunnelling went to Clarke, Devoret and Martinis, which overlaps in subject and may reduce appetite for another superconducting-circuit prize so soon.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed and widely adopted, though the recognition timing is complicated by the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits.
uncertainties: Four credited names but a maximum of three laureates, so Blais is excluded.
Recent related prize may make timing awkward.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres gave a room-temperature solid-state quantum sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and electric fields with nanoscale resolution, with uses in biology and materials. It is a clear case of a new measurement technique opening new observations.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko demonstrated single-NV optical detection and spin control; Lukin's group developed the quantum-sensing and register concepts. Credit relative to Gruber et al. (1997) and Awschalom, Hanson and Yacoby who also developed NV control may be a concern.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups worldwide and now partly moving to application, but practical sensitivities are still competing with established techniques and some applications are young.
uncertainties: Other major contributors (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Budker) are not in this set.
Real-world impact beyond demonstrations is still developing.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum cascade laser is a real invention built on bandgap engineering that gave compact mid-infrared sources, enabling trace-gas spectroscopy, sensing and some applications in defence and medicine. It is a case of an idea turned into a reliable device and widely used, which fits an experimentalist's priorities.
assessment.attribution: The 1994 demonstration at Bell Labs was led by Faist and Capasso with Cho's MBE growth; Kazarinov and Suris proposed the superlattice amplification concept earlier, which is an attribution issue outside the credited set. Three names are reasonable.
assessment.maturity: Mature and commercially established with thirty years of confirmation, so recognition is arguably overdue and not premature.
uncertainties: Early theoretical credit to Kazarinov and Suris is outside the credited names.
Whether the physics novelty versus engineering weight suits the prize.
